items.stem:
Read the following news report from a coastal newspaper in Kenya.

RECORD TURTLE HATCHING ON WATAMU BEACH
More than 1,200 green turtle hatchlings reached the sea from Watamu Beach on Saturday night, the highest number recorded in a single night since monitoring began in 1998.
Volunteers from Local Ocean Conservation guarded 14 nests for eight weeks.
"We were on our knees in the sand at 2 a.m., counting," said volunteer Amani Mwangi, 17. "Every single one made it past the crabs."
Experts warn that rising sand temperatures could reduce numbers in future years.

Analyse the effect of the inverted pyramid ending with the expert warning in the text.
items.answer: The inverted pyramid ending with the expert warning: less essential but important context comes last, adding balance to the good news.
items.markingKey: The inverted pyramid ending with the expert warning: less essential but important context comes last, adding balance to the good news. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: "The most exciting part of a news story should be saved for the end." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: News uses the inverted pyramid: the most important facts come first; suspense is for stories, not reports.
items.markingKey: News uses the inverted pyramid: the most important facts come first; suspense is for stories, not reports. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The inverted pyramid is outdated in the age of online news."
items.answer: The inverted pyramid remains useful because online readers often read only the opening, though features and longer pieces use other structures.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: online readers scroll and skim; some sites prefer storytelling openings. Arguments against: skimming readers need key facts first; it suits headlines and notifications. Supported judgement: The inverted pyramid remains useful because online readers often read only the opening, though features and longer pieces use other structures.

items.stem:
Read the following news report from an online news site in Pakistan.

TEENAGERS' APP HELPS RESCUERS REACH FLOOD FAMILIES
A free app built by three students from Lahore has helped rescue teams locate more than 400 families cut off by floods in Sindh province this week.
The app, called Pukaar ("Call"), lets users share their location and needs even with a weak signal.
"We built it in a weekend," said co-founder Hira Baig, 16. "We didn't sleep much."
Rescue coordinator Imran Shah called the app "a lifeline", but warned that thousands of people still have no phone access at all.

Identify one fact and one opinion in the text.
items.answer: Fact: "has helped rescue teams locate more than 400 families". Opinion: Imran Shah's description of the app as "a lifeline" (a judgement, attributed to him).
items.markingKey: Fact: "has helped rescue teams locate more than 400 families". Opinion: Imran Shah's description of the app as "a lifeline" (a judgement, attributed to him). items.stem:
Text A: report in a local newspaper about a new skatepark (Report A).

YOUTH CELEBRATE AS SKATEPARK FINALLY OPENS
Hundreds of young people cheered on Saturday as Riverside Skatepark opened after a three-year campaign by local teenagers.
"This is ours. We fought for it," said Lina Osei, 15, who collected 2,000 signatures.
The council spent €180,000 on the park, which includes ramps, a bowl and free lessons for beginners.
Councillor Mark Dubois called it "an investment in our young people".

Text B: report in a local newspaper about a new skatepark (Report B).

RESIDENTS FEAR NOISE AS €180,000 SKATEPARK OPENS
Residents near Riverside Park have complained about noise and litter after a new skatepark opened on Saturday.
"We can't hear our own television," said retired teacher Joan Price, 72. "And who's paying for this? We are."
The council spent €180,000 on the facility despite cuts to street lighting this year.
Young people, who campaigned for the park, were not available for comment.

Identify ONE similarity and ONE difference between the two texts, supporting each with a reference to both texts.
items.answer: Similarity: both include the same fact that the council spent €180,000 and that the park opened on Saturday. Difference: Text A quotes only supporters and celebrates the opening, while Text B quotes only a resident who complains and leaves out young people.
items.markingKey: Similarity: both include the same fact that the council spent €180,000 and that the park opened on Saturday. Difference: Text A quotes only supporters and celebrates the opening, while Text B quotes only a resident who complains and leaves out young people. One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

Read the following news report from a coastal newspaper in Kenya.

RECORD TURTLE HATCHING ON WATAMU BEACH
More than 1,200 green turtle hatchlings reached the sea from Watamu Beach on Saturday night, the highest number recorded in a single night since monitoring began in 1998.
Volunteers from Local Ocean Conservation guarded 14 nests for eight weeks.
"We were on our knees in the sand at 2 a.m., counting," said volunteer Amani Mwangi, 17. "Every single one made it past the crabs."
Experts warn that rising sand temperatures could reduce numbers in future years.

Separate fact from opinion in this report, giving one example of each.
items.answer: Fact: "Volunteers from Local Ocean Conservation guarded 14 nests for eight weeks." Opinion or prediction: "Experts warn that rising sand temperatures could reduce numbers" (a forecast, not yet proved).
items.markingKey: Fact: "Volunteers from Local Ocean Conservation guarded 14 nests for eight weeks." Opinion or prediction: "Experts warn that rising sand temperatures could reduce numbers" (a forecast, not yet proved). Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Ana writes: "The most exciting part of a news story should be saved for the end." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: News uses the inverted pyramid: the most important facts come first; suspense is for stories, not reports.
items.markingKey: News uses the inverted pyramid: the most important facts come first; suspense is for stories, not reports. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following report in a local newspaper about a new skatepark (Report B).

RESIDENTS FEAR NOISE AS €180,000 SKATEPARK OPENS
Residents near Riverside Park have complained about noise and litter after a new skatepark opened on Saturday.
"We can't hear our own television," said retired teacher Joan Price, 72. "And who's paying for this? We are."
The council spent €180,000 on the facility despite cuts to street lighting this year.
Young people, who campaigned for the park, were not available for comment.

Identify the technique in "Young people ... were not available for comment" and explain why a headline writer might use it.
items.answer: Omission: "Young people ... were not available for comment" – leaving out the teenagers' voice makes the report one-sided.
items.markingKey: Omission: "Young people ... were not available for comment" – leaving out the teenagers' voice makes the report one-sided. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following report in a local newspaper about a new skatepark (Report A).

YOUTH CELEBRATE AS SKATEPARK FINALLY OPENS
Hundreds of young people cheered on Saturday as Riverside Skatepark opened after a three-year campaign by local teenagers.
"This is ours. We fought for it," said Lina Osei, 15, who collected 2,000 signatures.
The council spent €180,000 on the park, which includes ramps, a bowl and free lessons for beginners.
Councillor Mark Dubois called it "an investment in our young people".

Separate fact from opinion in this report, giving one example of each.
items.answer: Fact: "The council spent €180,000 on the park". Opinion: "an investment in our young people" (Councillor Dubois's judgement).
items.markingKey: Fact: "The council spent €180,000 on the park". Opinion: "an investment in our young people" (Councillor Dubois's judgement). Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: "Numbers in news reports are always neutral." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Numbers can be framed to create impressions, e.g. putting "€180,000" in a headline beside "fear" suggests waste.
items.markingKey: Numbers can be framed to create impressions, e.g. putting "€180,000" in a headline beside "fear" suggests waste. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Put these parts of a news report in inverted-pyramid order: (a) background on previous competitions; (b) the result and who won; (c) a quotation from the team captain.
items.answer: (b) result – (c) quotation – (a) background.
items.markingKey: (b) result – (c) quotation – (a) background.

items.stem:
Read the following set of newspaper headlines.

1. "PURR-FECT ENDING: CAT FOUND AFTER 3 WEEKS UP CRANE"
2. "Mayor's Mega Mall Madness"
3. "Thugs Trash Park in Night of Shame"
4. "Students Spark Clean-Up Revolution"
5. "Heatwave: 40°C Recorded in Seville"

Compare the language choices in these headlines. Which is most neutral and which is most loaded?
items.answer: Headline 1 uses a pun ("PURR-FECT") for humour; headline 2 uses alliteration ("Mayor's Mega Mall Madness") and the loaded word "Madness" to mock a decision; headline 3 uses loaded words ("Thugs", "Shame") to condemn; headline 4 uses a positive metaphor ("Spark ... Revolution"); headline 5 is neutral and factual.
items.markingKey: Headline 1 uses a pun ("PURR-FECT") for humour; headline 2 uses alliteration ("Mayor's Mega Mall Madness") and the loaded word "Madness" to mock a decision; headline 3 uses loaded words ("Thugs", "Shame") to condemn; headline 4 uses a positive metaphor ("Spark ... Revolution"); headline 5 is neutral and factual. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "It is impossible for any news report to be completely unbiased."
items.answer: Complete neutrality is very difficult because selection is unavoidable, but reports can be more or less balanced; readers should compare sources.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: journalists must select information; word choice always has connotations. Arguments against: professional standards aim for balance; quoting several sides reduces bias. Supported judgement: Complete neutrality is very difficult because selection is unavoidable, but reports can be more or less balanced; readers should compare sources.

items.stem: "The inverted pyramid is outdated in the age of online news." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The inverted pyramid remains useful because online readers often read only the opening, though features and longer pieces use other structures.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: online readers scroll and skim; some sites prefer storytelling openings. Arguments against: skimming readers need key facts first; it suits headlines and notifications. Supported judgement: The inverted pyramid remains useful because online readers often read only the opening, though features and longer pieces use other structures. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "Clever headlines are more important than accurate ones." Discuss.
items.answer: Accuracy matters more, because many readers never read beyond the headline; wit is valuable only when it does not mislead.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: clever headlines attract readers; competition for clicks. Arguments against: misleading headlines damage trust; many readers only read the headline.
